info.bio: Projecto musical de Daniel Miller, fundador y dueño de Mute Records (NON, Depeche Mode, Nick Cave, Diamanda Galas, Laibach, Erasure, Goldfrapp, Throbbing Gristle, Fad Gadget, DAF,...). En 1978, Daniel Miller publicaría un single con los temas T.V.O.D y Warm Leatherette, unico trabajo del proyecto que abandonaría tras realizar unos pocos conciertos para pasar a ser productor y gestor de la mítica companía inglesa de música electrónica y vanguardista Mute Records.

scenes.name: Electrónica casera: The Normal y Mute
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Contagiado por las Desperate Bicycles, Daniel Miller compra un Korg usado y graba en su cuarto «T.V.O.D.»/«Warm Leatherette» como The Normal: electropunk de puñaladas de sintetizador y erotismo de accidentes de coche a lo Crash de Ballard. Vende treinta mil copias y le convierte en director de Mute (Fad Gadget). A mediados de 1978 coinciden otros singles electrónicos lo-fi de sellos indie: «United» de Throbbing Gristle, Extended Play de Cabaret Voltaire, «Being Boiled» de The Human League, «Paralysis» de Robert Rental y «Private Plane» de Thomas Leer, hecho sin sintetizador y susurrado para no despertar a su novia.

scenes.name: Punk electrónico
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: «Hazlo tú mismo, pero con sintetizadores»: el punk aporta energía y autogestión, y los Korg y Roland japoneses abaratan la tecnología. Daniel Miller funda Mute con The Normal («un cruce entre Ramones y Kraftwerk») y la banda fantasma Silicon Teens; siguen Fad Gadget, Robert Rental, Thomas Leer y DAF.

podcast.title: Bedroom Punk Aesthetic with Synthesizers
podcast.body: Daniel Miller, aspiring to be a punk but unable to play guitar, bought a Korg 700S and a 4-track reel-to-reel machine from his film editor savings. He recorded "Warm Leatherette" in his bedroom, creating a minimalist, futuristic sound with attitude, which sold 30,000 copies. This demonstrated that musical experience wasn't necessary for creating impactful electronic music, embodying a punk sensibility of DIY attitude over traditional ability. "He started experimenting with it in his bedroom. Recorded two songs, found some money to make a test pressing and convinced the rough-trade record shop in Notting Hill to stock it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bedroom Recording Pioneer
podcast.body: Daniel Miller, the sole member of The Normal, composed and recorded the single "Warm Leatherette" in his bedroom in 1978, showcasing the accessibility of electronic music production. "Daniel Miller, the solitary member of a band known as The Normal from 1978 with Warm Leatherette, a single that became a substantial UK hit that year, and a song that was composed and recorded in Daniel's bedroom."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding Mute Records
podcast.body: Using the profits from "Warm Leatherette," Daniel Miller established his own independent record label, Mute, dedicated exclusively to guitar-less music, which later introduced artists like Depeche Mode, Erasure, and Yazoo. "He took the profits and founded his own independent record label devoted entirely to guitar less music. He called the label Mute."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding Mute Records
podcast.body: Daniel Miller created Mute Records in his bedroom in 1978 as the only way to generate interest in his one-man synth band project, The Normal. He secured a deal with Rough Trade Record Shops for distribution. "Mute records, which was started by a kid named Daniel Miller in his bedroom in 1978. He had a one-man synth band project called The Normal. And the only way he could interest anyone in what he was doing was to do it all himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

podcast.title: Funding Mute Records Expansion
podcast.body: The money generated from the sale of 30,000 copies of The Normal's seven-inch single, "Warm Leatherette," was reinvested by Daniel Miller into Mute Records, which eventually led to his collaboration with Depeche Mode. "Daniel took the money from that single Warm Leatherette by The Normal and plowed it back into mute, which eventually saw him cross paths with Depeche Mode."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

podcast.title: Independent Sales Success
podcast.body: After recording "Warm Leatherette" in his bedroom, Miller sold 30,000 copies by placing it for sale on consignment in independent record stores. "And just by putting it for sale on consignment and independent record stores, Daniel sold 30,000 copies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influenced by Bowie and Kraftwerk
podcast.body: Miller was influenced by the electronic music of David Bowie and Kraftwerk, combining the concept of stylish, futuristic, machine-generated music with punk rock's DIY aesthetic. "Like a number of young British musicians, Miller had been exposed to craft work and the electronic musings of David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Minimalist Sound as a Contrast
podcast.body: The minimalist sound of Daniel Miller's "Warm Leatherette" served as a benchmark against which the later, more sonically advanced and textured Technopop songs from 1980-81 were compared, highlighting the rapid technological progress in a short period. "Remember what warm leatherettes sounded like? Now compare that minimalism to something like this, which came out less than two years ago."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Production of "I Feel Love" (1977)
xref.body: Giorgio Moroder produced Donna Summer's 1977 track "I Feel Love," which became known as the first truly computerized and synthesized dance single. His work on this track incorporated elements that later influenced artists like Daniel Miller of The Normal. "That was the first truly computerized, slashed synthesized dance single, which she created with the help of producer George Eomeroder."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Creator of The Normal and "Warm Leatherette" (1978)
xref.body: Daniel Miller was the driving force behind the group The Normal, and he crafted the song "Warm Leatherette" (November 1978) by drawing inspiration from Kraftwerk, Lou Reed, and Giorgio Moroder. This composition contributed to the emerging "cold wave" sound. "Daniel Miller, who's the guy behind the normal, took some elements of craft work, Lou Reed and George Eomeroder, to create this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Enlarged Heart
xref.body: The early report following Taylor Hawkins' death stated that his heart was enlarged, weighing 600 grams, which is twice the normal size for a person of his age and size. An enlarged heart is a symptom of various underlying conditions and, if untreated, can lead to serious cardiac issues including sudden cardiac arrest. "The early report also said that Taylor's heart was enlarged."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influential Robotic Sound
xref.body: Kraftwerk's music from the late 1970s, exemplified by "The Model," was characterized by a robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and intense vibe. This sound was a significant part of early Technopop and greatly intrigued and influenced artists like David Bowie. "And note the vibe of that song. Much of early technopop was robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and just generally a little intense. That description can also be applied to craft work, the normal and some of Bowie's electronic experiments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robotic Electronic Experiments
xref.body: Some of David Bowie's electronic experiments exhibited a similar robotic, cold, artificial, emotionally sterile, and intense vibe to early Technopop artists like Kraftwerk and The Normal. This aesthetic characterized a significant portion of the emerging electronic music scene. "That description can also be applied to craft work, the normal and some of Bowie's electronic experiments."
